title: State of AI Models & Prices
dek_2026: What frontier AI models can do and what they cost: benchmark scores, the US–China and open–closed gaps, token prices from the cheapest tier to the frontier, training compute and cost, context windows, reasoning milestones and energy per query, each dated and sourced.

metrics.label: SWE-bench Verified, top reported score

2024.source: OpenAI (o3 preview announcement), as reported in Stanford HAI AI Index 2025
2024.note: o3 was a preview, not generally available, when this score was announced. Stanford HAI pairs it with a 4.4% 2023 figure that was measured on the original full SWE-bench, not SWE-bench Verified (released Aug 2024); the two endpoints are different test versions. Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Oct 2024) was the best generally available model at about 49%.

2025.note: First model reported above 80%. Rivals at the time: GPT-5.1-Codex-Max 77.9%, Claude Sonnet 4.5 77.2%, Gemini 3 Pro 76.2% (vendor figures, secondary reporting).

2026.source: Vals.ai SWE-bench Verified leaderboard (Claude Opus 5, mini-SWE-agent harness)
2026.note: Single independent harness, read via search summary. DeepSeek V4 Pro 96.4% and GPT-5.6 Sol 96.2% on the same board. BenchLM (29 Jul 2026) shows 96%; vendor figure for Claude Opus 4.8 was 88.6% (May 2026, page 964). Vals says the benchmark is saturated and no longer runs it on new releases. Stanford HAI 2026 describes the same move as about 60% to nearly 100% of the human baseline in one year. Harness differences mean 2026 is not strictly comparable with the vendor-run 2024–25 figures.

2024.note: Vendor-reported for a preview model; not re-verified in this session. Generally available o1 (Sep–Dec 2024) reported 78%. Stanford HAI records a +48.9 percentage-point one-year gain on GPQA, 2023 to 2024.

2025.note: GPT-5.2 Pro reported 93.2% and Gemini 3 Pro 91.9% in the same period (secondary reporting of vendor figures).

2026.note: An aggregator lists GPT-5.4 Pro at 94.4% (self-reported). Expert review suggests only about 90–95% of GPQA Diamond questions are valid, so scores in the mid-90s are at the ceiling: the benchmark is saturated.

2024: Stanford HAI's AI Index 2025 found that the inference price of GPT-3.5-level performance fell from $20 per million tokens in November 2022 to $0.07 in October 2024, a more than 280-fold decline.
The ARC Prize Foundation reported on 20 December 2024 that OpenAI's o3 preview scored 75.7% on the ARC-AGI-1 semi-private evaluation within the $10,000 compute limit.
OpenAI reported in December 2024 that its o3 preview resolved 71.7% of SWE-bench Verified coding tasks, a figure Stanford HAI uses as the 2024 high point.
Stanford HAI counted 40 notable AI models from US institutions in 2024, against 15 from China and 3 from Europe.

On the Chatbot Arena leaderboard in January 2024, the top closed-weight model led the best open-weight model by 8.04% and the top US model led the best Chinese model by 9.26%, according to Stanford HAI's AI Index 2025.
2025: Anthropic reported that Claude Opus 4.5, released on 24 November 2025, scored 80.9% on SWE-bench Verified, the first model reported above 80%.
Google DeepMind's Gemini Deep Think scored 35 of 42 points at the July 2025 International Mathematical Olympiad, the first AI result officially certified at gold-medal standard.
Epoch AI estimated that training xAI's Grok 4, released in July 2025, used about 5×10^26 FLOP and cost about $490 million, the largest known training run.
DeepSeek priced its open-weight R1 reasoning model at $0.55 per million input tokens and $2.19 per million output tokens on 20 January 2025, against $15 and $60 for OpenAI's o1.
Stanford HAI's 2026 AI Index reports that the median price per million tokens across AI models fell from $2.10 in 2024 to $0.85 in 2025.
2026: Vals.ai's SWE-bench Verified leaderboard, updated on 1 September 2026, ranked Claude Opus 5 first at 97.0%, and Vals said the benchmark had saturated.

Stanford HAI's 2026 AI Index found that the top US model led the best Chinese model by 2.7% on the Arena leaderboard in March 2026, and the top closed-weight model led the best open-weight model by 3.3%.

Silicon Data's usage-weighted LLM Token Expenditure Index fell to $0.97 per million tokens on 1 September 2026, while Anthropic's top model, Claude Fable 5.1, listed at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens.
The ARC Prize Foundation verified a score of 84.6% on ARC-AGI-2 for Google's Gemini 3 Deep Think in February 2026, up from a verified best of 54% in December 2025.

Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5, launched on 7 October 2026, lists at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens for prompts up to 100,000 tokens, a tenth of Claude Haiku 4.5's $1 and $5.

2024: 2024 was the year the classic capability benchmarks broke. Stanford HAI's AI Index 2025 recorded one-year gains of 48.9 percentage points on GPQA and 18.8 on MMMU between 2023 and 2024. In December, OpenAI's o3 preview posted 71.7% on SWE-bench Verified and, according to the ARC Prize Foundation, 75.7% on the ARC-AGI-1 semi-private set within the public compute limit. Both December results came from a model that was not yet available to customers, which matters: the year-end frontier was a preview, not a product. MMLU, the reference test since 2020, effectively stopped separating models once OpenAI's o1 reported 92.3% in September 2024, close to the test's practical ceiling of about 95%.

Prices fell faster than capability rose. Stanford HAI measured the cost of GPT-3.5-level performance (MMLU 64.8) at $0.07 per million tokens in October 2024, down from $20 in November 2022, a decline of more than 280-fold. That curve describes a fixed capability bar, not the price of the newest model. OpenAI's o1 launched in December 2024 at $15 per million input tokens and $60 per million output tokens, and Anthropic's top model, Claude 3 Opus, listed at $15 and $75. The pattern that runs through this whole series was already visible: last year's capability became nearly free while the frontier was priced for what buyers would pay.

The competitive map narrowed from two sides. On the Chatbot Arena leaderboard in January 2024 the top closed-weight model led the best open-weight model by 8.04% and the top US model led the best Chinese model by 9.26%; DeepSeek-V3, released on 26 December 2024 under open weights, closed much of both gaps within weeks. Output still favoured the US, which produced 40 notable models in 2024 to China's 15 and Europe's 3 (Stanford HAI). Training budgets kept climbing: the AI Index's widely cited estimate for Meta's Llama 3.1 405B is about $170 million, and Epoch AI's records show no model above 10^26 FLOP of training compute until Grok 3 in February 2025.
2025: 2025 was the year test-time compute became the main lever of progress. DeepSeek-R1, released on 20 January, showed that reinforcement-learned reasoning could be reproduced with open weights at a fraction of o1's price: $0.55 and $2.19 per million input and output tokens against $15 and $60. In July, Gemini Deep Think earned an officially certified gold-medal score of 35 out of 42 at the International Mathematical Olympiad, up from a 28-point silver for DeepMind's formal-proof systems in 2024. By year-end, Claude Opus 4.5 had become the first model reported above 80% on SWE-bench Verified (80.9%, 24 November) and Gemini 3 Deep Think reported 93.8% on GPQA Diamond, close to that test's ceiling.

As older tests saturated, attention moved to benchmarks designed to resist them, and those moved quickly too. Humanity's Last Exam launched in January 2025 with the best models near 9%; OpenAI's Deep Research, which searches the web, reached 26.6% in February, and Gemini 3 Deep Think reported 41.0% without tools in December, though another account gives 45.1%. ARC-AGI-2, launched in March to replace the near-solved original, ended the year with a verified top score of 54% from Poetiq, a six-person startup running its own system on top of Gemini 3 Pro. Scores on these tests depend heavily on the setting, with or without tools and verified or self-reported, and should not be compared across settings.

Training costs and usage prices moved in opposite directions. Epoch AI estimates that xAI's Grok 4, released in July, used about 5×10^26 FLOP, the largest known run, at a median cost of about $490 million. Meanwhile Stanford HAI's 2026 AI Index reports that the median price per million tokens across models fell from $2.10 in 2024 to $0.85 in 2025, and Epoch measured price declines at fixed capability with a median of about 50× a year. Anthropic cut its flagship price by two-thirds when Opus 4.5 launched at $5 and $25 per million tokens. Model output stayed concentrated: the US produced 50 notable models to China's 30 in 2025 by the AI Index's chapter count, while a later Stanford page gives 59 and 35.
2026: By 2026 the benchmarks that defined the previous two years were effectively exhausted. Vals.ai's SWE-bench Verified board, updated on 1 September 2026, showed Claude Opus 5 at 97.0%, with DeepSeek V4 Pro and GPT-5.6 Sol within one point, and Vals stopped running the test on new releases. GPQA Diamond topped out near 94%, roughly the share of its questions that experts judge valid. The ARC Prize Foundation verified 84.6% on ARC-AGI-2 for Gemini 3 Deep Think in February. Even the International Mathematical Olympiad stopped separating models: several systems were reported with perfect 42-point scores in July, though they were not graded the same way and we found no official IMO certification. The measurable frontier now sits on Humanity's Last Exam, ARC-AGI-3 and agentic tests.

The frontier is crowded and the gaps are small, but not zero. Stanford HAI's 2026 AI Index puts the top US model's lead over the best Chinese model at 2.7% on the Arena leaderboard in March 2026, and the closed-weight lead over open weights at 3.3%, wider than the 1.70% recorded in February 2025. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index in September, Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Max scored 58 against 58.9 for OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol. How large the open-weight gap looks depends on the instrument: about 6 points on Artificial Analysis's index in September, 12 points on its stricter version 5 in October, roughly 26 if only models with published weights are counted, and about four months of lag by Epoch AI's measure.

Prices now move in two directions. Silicon Data's usage-weighted index, which tracks what the market actually pays, fell to $0.97 per million tokens on 1 September 2026 and below $1 again in October, about 54% under its late-May peak of $2.07. New small models launched at a tenth of their predecessors' prices: Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 lists at $0.10 input and $0.50 output per million tokens, against $1 and $5 for Haiku 4.5. At the top, prices are holding or rising. Claude Fable 5.1 lists at $10 and $50, and Google's Gemini 4 Argon doubles to $4 and $20 when its introductory period ends on 30 November 2026. Cheap capability is getting cheaper; the frontier is being priced as scarce.

Two things got harder to measure. Public estimates of training compute and cost for closed models largely stop after mid-2025, because labs disclose less: Stanford HAI reports that the average Foundation Model Transparency Index score fell from 58 to 40. And availability became a variable in its own right. Anthropic withdrew Claude Fable 5 under US export controls within a week of its 9 June launch, and OpenAI paused its largest planned reinforcement-learning run in August after evaluations could not rule out a critical cyber-risk level. Energy per query is the one cost that still looks small, about 0.31 watt-hours for a median chatbot query in a 2026 Microsoft Research study, but the same study puts long reasoning responses near 3.9 Wh, which is where usage is heading.

takeaways_2026: The classic benchmarks are saturated: SWE-bench Verified reached 97.0% (Vals.ai, 1 Sep 2026), GPQA Diamond about 94% (Feb 2026) and perfect IMO scores were reported in July 2026; real separation now shows only on Humanity's Last Exam (about 55–60%, contested) and ARC-AGI-3 (below 1%).

The gaps are small but depend on the instrument: Stanford HAI measured a 2.7% US lead over China and a 3.3% closed-over-open lead on Arena in March 2026, while Artificial Analysis's open-weight gap ranged from 6 to 26 points across versions and definitions in September–October 2026.

Prices run at two speeds: the usage-weighted market price fell below $1 per million tokens (Silicon Data, Sep–Oct 2026) and Anthropic's smallest model got 90% cheaper, while frontier list prices sit between $4/$20 and $10/$50 and Google's Gemini 4 Argon doubles its price on 30 November 2026.

The cost side of frontier AI has gone dark: Epoch AI's ~$490 million estimate for Grok 4 (2025) is the last solid training-cost figure, transparency scores fell from 58 to 40 (Stanford HAI), and a US export order showed in June 2026 that a released model can be withdrawn within a week.
yoy_takeaways: Coding: the top SWE-bench Verified score went from 71.7% (o3 preview, Dec 2024) to 80.9% (Claude Opus 4.5, Nov 2025) to 97.0% (Claude Opus 5, Sep 2026, independent harness) — saturated in under two years.

Competition: the top US model's Arena lead over China went 9.26% (Jan 2024) → 1.70% (Feb 2025) → 2.7% (Mar 2026), and the closed-over-open lead 8.04% → 1.70% → 3.3%: convergence, then a modest reopening.

Frontier prices: Anthropic's Opus-tier output price fell from $75 (2024) to $25 (2025) to $20 per million tokens (2026), and OpenAI's newest flagship from $60 (o1) to $10 (GPT-5, GPT-6 Sol) — but a new top tier appeared above Opus at $50 (Claude Fable 5.1).
Reasoning: AI went from a 28/42 silver at the 2024 IMO to a certified 35/42 gold in 2025 to reported perfect 42/42 scores in 2026.

faq_2026.q: What is the best AI model in November 2026?
faq_2026.a: It depends on the test and the month. On Artificial Analysis's version 5 Intelligence Index in October 2026, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 led at 58. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra led Scale's Humanity's Last Exam leaderboard at 54.8% on 17 October 2026, and Claude Opus 5 topped Vals.ai's SWE-bench Verified board at 97.0% on 1 September 2026. Google says Gemini 4 Argon, generally available since 13 October 2026, leads 12 or 13 of 18 benchmarks, but those are its own evaluations. No single model leads on every measure.

faq_2026.q: How much does it cost to use an AI model in 2026?
faq_2026.a: It depends on the tier. Silicon Data's usage-weighted index, which reflects what the market actually pays, was $0.97 per million tokens on 1 September 2026 and fell below $1 again in October. Small models are cheapest: Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens (7 October 2026). Frontier models cost far more: OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol lists at $2 and $10 (22 September 2026), Claude Opus 5.5 at $4 and $20, Claude Fable 5.1 at $10 and $50, and Google's Gemini 4 Argon rises to $4 and $20 after 30 November 2026.

faq_2026.q: Has China caught up with the US in AI models?
faq_2026.a: Nearly, on capability. Stanford HAI's 2026 AI Index found the top US model led the best Chinese model by 2.7% on the Arena leaderboard in March 2026, down from 9.26% in January 2024. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index on 3 September 2026, Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Max scored 58 against 58.9 for OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol. The US still produces more notable models: 50 to China's 30 in 2025 by one Stanford count (59 to 35 by another), up from 40 to 15 in 2024. China's distinctive advantage is open weights; its labs publish them and the leading US labs mostly do not.

faq_2026.q: Are open-weight AI models as good as closed ones in 2026?
faq_2026.a: Close, but behind, and how far behind depends on the measure. Stanford HAI found the top closed model led the best open model by 3.3% on Arena in March 2026, up from 1.70% in February 2025. Epoch AI estimates open-weight models have lagged the closed frontier by about four months on average since January 2026. On Artificial Analysis's index the gap was about 6 points in September 2026, but 12 points on its stricter version 5 in October, and about 26 points if only models with published weights are counted.

faq_2026.q: How much energy does one AI query use in 2026?
faq_2026.a: A typical text query uses roughly a third of a watt-hour. A 2026 Microsoft Research study in the journal Joule estimated a median of 0.31 watt-hours per chatbot query, in line with Google's August 2025 figure of 0.24 Wh for a median Gemini text prompt and Sam Altman's June 2025 figure of about 0.34 Wh for ChatGPT. Long reasoning-style responses use far more: about 3.9 Wh in the same study. The older 2.9 Wh per-query figure from 2023–24 is out of date, and no regulator requires companies to disclose these numbers.

stop_quoting.claim: AI coding went from 4.4% to 71.7% on SWE-bench in one year.
stop_quoting.fact: The direction is right, but the two endpoints are different tests: 4.4% is a 2023 result on the original full SWE-bench, while 71.7% is OpenAI's o3 preview on SWE-bench Verified, a human-validated 500-task subset released in August 2024, announced in December 2024 before o3 was available. Quote each with its test version and date. This pairing appears on Report AI pages 89, 322, 386 and 413 and should carry that caveat.

Stanford HAI's 280× figure is the price of reaching GPT-3.5-level performance, from $20 per million tokens in November 2022 to $0.07 in October 2024. It describes a fixed, old capability bar, not frontier prices, which in 2026 range from $2/$10 (GPT-6 Sol) to $10/$50 (Claude Fable 5.1) per million input/output tokens.

stop_quoting.claim: AI now costs less than $1 per million tokens.
stop_quoting.fact: Silicon Data's $0.97 reading (1 September 2026) is a usage-weighted average dominated by cheap and mid-tier models. It is what the market pays on average, not what frontier capability costs; frontier list prices are 4 to 50 times higher on output.

stop_quoting.claim: One AI query uses about 3 watt-hours, ten times a Google search.
stop_quoting.fact: That 2.9 Wh estimate dates from 2023–24. Google reported 0.24 Wh for a median Gemini text prompt (August 2025) and a 2026 Microsoft Research study found a 0.31 Wh median. Long reasoning responses can reach about 3.9 Wh, so the high figure now applies only to that kind of query.

stop_quoting.claim: DeepSeek trained a frontier model for $5.6 million (or $294,000).
stop_quoting.fact: $5.58 million was DeepSeek's stated GPU-rental cost for the final pre-training run of V3; $294,000 was the reinforcement-learning stage that turned V3 into R1 (Nature, September 2025). Neither includes research, earlier runs, staff or hardware, so neither is comparable with Epoch AI's ~$490 million estimate for Grok 4.

stop_quoting.claim: Open-source models have caught up with closed models.
stop_quoting.fact: Stanford HAI measured a 3.3% closed-model lead on Arena in March 2026, wider than in 2025; Epoch AI puts the lag at about four months; and Artificial Analysis's version 5 index (October 2026) shows a 12-point gap, or about 26 points counting only models with published weights.

stop_quoting.claim: Claude Fable 5 is the world's best AI model (Intelligence Index 59.9).
stop_quoting.fact: Fable 5 was withdrawn under US export controls within a week of its 9 June 2026 launch, and the listed score may partly reflect its Opus 4.8 fallback. Any 'best model' claim needs a test name and a date.

stop_quoting.claim: The US produced 40 notable AI models last year.
stop_quoting.fact: 40 is the 2024 count (Stanford HAI AI Index 2025). For 2025 the AI Index 2026 gives 50 in its chapter PDF and 59 on its web page; China's count rose from 15 to 30 or 35.
